title: The Scar at His Throat
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 7 of 40
content:
The Auror sent by Kingsley Shacklebolt was young enough to look nervous in Severus Snape's presence and experienced enough to resent himself for it.

His name was Dawlish.

Not that Dawlish.

He clarified this before sitting down, which told me more about his professional life than he probably intended.

“My uncle,” he said. “Different branch.”

Snape's lip curled. “How reassuring.”

We had commandeered an unused classroom on the third floor. McGonagall had removed the desks and conjured a square table with four chairs. She sat at one end. The Auror sat at the other. I took the side nearest the window.

Snape remained standing.

“Sit,” McGonagall said.

“No.”

The Auror glanced at his notes.

I knew the real reason.

Snape's throat was bad that morning.

The scar looked angrier above his collar, and every few minutes he swallowed carefully as if the motion cost him. Sitting made him tilt his head in a way that tugged at the healing tissue. Standing let him control the angle.

I said nothing.

The interview began with the hidden cache.

“When did you first become aware of these potions?” the Auror asked.

“When the consultant found them.”

“Before that, you had no knowledge?”

“No.”

“You were Headmaster at the time they were likely hidden.”

“I am familiar with my former job title.”

McGonagall closed her eyes briefly.

The Auror continued. “Did Alecto Carrow have access to your stores?”

“Not with my permission.”

“But in practice?”

“In practice, she had the support of a homicidal government and a brother with poor impulse control.”

The quill scratched furiously.

I wondered how one spelled poor impulse control in official shorthand.

The questions moved to the six phials Snape had brewed for Voldemort.

“Your consultant believes you deliberately sabotaged them.”

“Your consultant?” Snape said.

The Auror flushed. “The school's consultant.”

“Then say so.”

I kicked Snape lightly beneath the table before remembering he was standing.

My foot hit empty air.

He noticed anyway.

His eyes flicked toward me.

I gave him a look.

He looked almost entertained.

“Yes,” he said. “They were sabotaged.”

“Why?”

“To prevent their intended function.”

“Why not refuse to brew them?”

Snape stared at him.

The young Auror held the stare for three seconds.

Then two.

Then looked down.

“Right,” he muttered.

The questioning continued.

At the forty-minute mark, Snape's voice roughened.

At fifty, he began answering in single words.

At fifty-five, a thin line of red appeared at the edge of his collar.

I was out of my chair before I thought about it.

“Stop.”

Everyone looked at me.

Snape's face became lethal.

“We're done for ten minutes,” I said.

“We are not.”

“You're bleeding.”

His hand went to his throat.

The Auror looked horrified.

McGonagall stood.

“Severus—”

“I am perfectly capable of—”

His voice failed.

Not weakened.

Failed.

The last word broke into air.

Silence filled the room.

Snape froze.

For the first time since I had met him, I saw fear arrive before he could hide it.

He turned away.

I did not touch him.

“Water?” I asked.

A curt nod.

I poured without commentary and held the glass where he could take it himself.

His hand shook once.

He drank.

McGonagall moved toward the door. “I am fetching Poppy.”

Snape caught her sleeve.

He shook his head.

“Then I will fetch the salve,” I said.

Another nod.

The Auror had gone pale.

“I can come back.”

Snape pointed at the door.

He came back two hours later.

By then Madam Pomfrey had applied salve, lectured Snape, lectured McGonagall for allowing the interview, and lectured me for not stopping it sooner. I accepted my portion. Snape did not accept his, but he endured it.

When everyone left, I remained in the classroom with him.

He wrote on a scrap of parchment.

GO.

“No.”

His quill stabbed the paper.

WHY?

“Because we have to walk back to the dungeon and you're dizzy.”

I AM NOT.

“You walked into a chair ten minutes ago.”

THE CHAIR MOVED.

I looked at him.

He looked back.

Even voiceless, Severus Snape could be sarcastic.

It was almost comforting.

“Fine. The chair attacked you. I'm still walking with you.”

He wrote something longer.

I leaned over.

YOUR CONTRACT DOES NOT INCLUDE ESCORTING INVALIDS THROUGH CORRIDORS.

I took the quill from his fingers before he could object.

GOOD THING YOU ARE NOT AN INVALID, I wrote beneath it.

His eyes narrowed.

I added: YOU ARE AN IRRITATING MAN WITH A TEMPORARY INJURY.

He stared at the sentence.

Then at me.

The expression on his face was so complicated I could not read it.

He stood.

We walked.

Slowly.

Portraits watched us pass. A few whispered. Snape ignored them with the concentrated skill of someone who had spent years being observed.

At the first staircase, he stopped to breathe.

I leaned against the opposite wall.

No fuss. No hand offered. No false conversation.

After a minute, he took out the scrap of parchment and wrote:

YOU ARE VERY BAD AT LEAVING PEOPLE ALONE.

“Actually, I'm excellent at it.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I am leaving you alone right now.”

YOU ARE THREE FEET AWAY.

“Emotionally, miles.”

His shoulders moved.

A silent laugh.

It made me absurdly happy.

Back in the dungeon, he went straight to his office. I assumed the day was over.

Then he reappeared carrying two cups of tea.

He placed one on my table.

I stared at it.

He wrote:

DO NOT MAKE THIS SIGNIFICANT.

“Wouldn't dream of it.”

The tea was strong and bitter with no sugar.

I drank it anyway.

Snape sat across from me. Without his voice, the room felt different. He could not control it through tone. Could not cut a conversation short with a syllable sharpened like a blade. He had only expression, gesture, and the furious scratch of his quill.

I wondered how much of his life had been built around a voice that made people back away.

He caught me looking at his throat.

His face hardened.

I looked at my cup.

A minute later, the parchment slid across the table.

ASK.

I looked up.

He tapped the word.

“You don't have to tell me anything.”

His eyes rolled.

He wrote:

I AM AWARE.

So I asked.

“Does it hurt all the time?”

A pause.

YES.

“How badly?”

VARIABLE.

“Will your voice recover?”

PROBABLY.

“That isn't very reassuring.”

NO.

I hesitated.

“Are you afraid it won't?”

The quill stopped.

His face emptied.

I thought he would end the conversation.

Instead he wrote one word.

YES.

Something in my chest tightened.

Not because a damaged voice was the worst thing he had survived. It was not. But because I understood suddenly how much control he placed in speech. Snape could make a room still by lowering his voice. He could hide pain inside precision. He could make cruelty sound like boredom and concern sound like insult.

Losing it was not only physical.

“It would be frightening,” I said.

His eyes lifted.

I did not say you'll be fine.

I did not say Pomfrey knows what she's doing.

I did not promise what neither of us could know.

“It makes sense that you're afraid.”

He stared at me for a very long time.

Then wrote:

I DETEST YOU.

I smiled.

“Better.”

His eyes narrowed.

I finished the tea.

He took the cup from me and returned both to his office.

When he came back, his posture was straighter.

He pointed at my unfinished inventory.

“You want to work?” I asked.

He nodded.

“Silently?”

A look.

“Right. Redundant question.”

We sorted ingredients for three hours without speaking.

It was one of the easiest afternoons we had spent together.

He communicated with taps of his wand, gestures, and increasingly insulting notes.

I learned that two taps meant wrong shelf.

Three meant absolutely not.

A flat stare meant I had done something correctly and he resented it.

Near the end of the day, I opened a jar of powdered valerian and sneezed.

Snape wrote something quickly and pushed it toward me.

WEAK.

I wrote beneath it:

ALIVE.

He read the word.

His expression changed.

Only for a second.

Then he folded the parchment in half and put it in his pocket.

I pretended not to notice.

Some things did not need to become evidence.
